content: The response to the HIV epidemic in El Salvador is being monitored through a unified HIV case reporting surveillance system known as SUMEVE (Sistema Unificado de Monitoreo y Evaluación de VIH en El Salvador). Over the past few years, this system has undergone significant advancements and is now fully digitized. SUMEVE is a web-based application that has been collecting nominal data since 2009. It tracks individuals with positive HIV test results from any type of health service, confirms HIV diagnoses, monitors clinical follow-ups, and records antiretroviral (ARV) drug prescriptions for treatment. Between 2015 and 2016, the HIV surveillance system was enhanced to identify gaps in care and treatment at the level of individual health centers and provinces. This improvement aimed to enhance the quality of care for people living with HIV. Using SUMEVE’s cascade analysis, gaps in each stage of the care continuum were identified. For instance, among the more than 17,000 registered and living HIV cases, 73% were linked to care, 54% were retained in care, 50% were receiving treatment, and 41% achieved viral load suppression (73% of those on treatment had viral suppression). The system also enables cascade analysis by gender, and unique identifiers are being introduced to allow for analysis by key populations. To further improve HIV services, the following recommendations are emphasized: 1. Promote and Use Unique Identifiers: Replace patient names in shared HIV records with anonymous unique identifiers linked to health records. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides definitions and examples of such identifiers. 2. Transition to Electronic Systems: Gradually shift from paper-based to electronic patient information systems, particularly in facilities with more than 2,000 patients. WHO suggests a tiered approach for this transition. 3. Strengthen Data Security: Establish and assess different levels of data security for various data elements. Invest in robust databases and policies to protect confidentiality and security based on risks and benefits in specific settings. 4. Invest in Data Systems and Interoperability: Countries should invest in secure and interoperable data systems, adopting open-source standards. WHO recommends allocating 5–10% of program budgets to strengthen monitoring and evaluation. 5. Leverage Individual Data for Program Improvement: Link data to program improvements and collect evidence of these enhancements. Strengthen retention and transfer of care by routinely sharing information between clinics, testing, treatment, laboratories, pharmacies, and other health services. 6. Integrate HIV Services with Chronic Health Care: Use unique identifiers to link HIV services with broader health services, ensuring continuity of care. 7. Build Data Analysis Capacity: Invest in data analysts at central and district levels and implement real-time dashboards to provide feedback for program improvement. Unique identifiers are critical for person-centered monitoring of HIV services. These identifiers are numeric or alphanumeric codes that allow individuals to be accurately identified across various health services while maintaining anonymity. This approach supports the transition from service-centered to person-centered data, improving care quality and facilitating data linkages as individuals move between health services and facilities. The use of unique identifiers enhances the effectiveness and efficiency of both case surveillance and patient monitoring. It allows for better linkage of testing and treatment, improved retention in care, reduced duplication of records, and enhanced program management. The transition to electronic health records and unique identifiers involves three stages: 1. Early Stage: Transition from name-based records to unique identifiers in paper-based systems. 2. Middle Stage: Widespread use of unique identifiers and deployment of electronic systems with a mix of online and offline elements. 3. Advanced Stage: Fully online electronic health information systems linked across services, facilities, and community care. The benefits of unique identifiers include improved continuity of care, enhanced retention and follow-up, better program efficiency, and evidence-based decision-making. In summary, the implementation of unique identifiers and electronic health systems is essential for person-centered HIV monitoring.
